title: The rest of the poem
hookLine: the full poem survives in Tibetan and Chinese, carrying the story to the relics

lines: A BOOK WITH ITS LAST PAGES GONE.
cards: A book with its last chapters torn out, and a friend overseas who happens to own a copy. That's roughly the situation with this poem.

The Sanskrit text, the language Ashvaghosha wrote in, breaks off partway through the story. If that were all there was, the life in verse would stop in the middle of the night under the tree, before the dawn.
But the poem was carried abroad and translated, into Tibetan and into Chinese, and in those versions the story keeps going, all the way to the end.

teach.b: So what's in the rest of the poem? Four stretches. First, a gift of land.
A rich merchant, Anathapindika, buys a prince's grove for the Buddha and the monks, so they have a place to stay through the rains. The teaching has a home. Second, the return.

The Buddha goes back to his father's city, the one he left through the silent gates. The king who tried to keep him in meets a son who comes back as a teacher, and listens. Third, the trouble and the welcome.
A cousin, Devadatta, turns against him and sets a maddened elephant loose in his path, and the elephant stops and grows calm before him.
And a courtesan, Amrapali, welcomes him into her mango grove and gives it to the community. The poem honors her gift. Fourth, the end.

teach.h: THE SALA TREES, AND THE RELICS SHARED.
teach.b: The Buddha, old and ill, makes his last journey, lies down between two sala trees at Kushinagara, gives his last teaching, and passes into final nirvana.
Near its close the poem goes one step further than the death: the kings of the region quarrel over his relics, nearly go to war, and then agree to share them, each carrying a portion home to honor.
So the story closes with the life scattered across many places, and kept. Notice the echo. The poem had the same fate: scattered, carried, kept in other languages.
This week ran from Mara's bow of flowers, through his defeat, the night of knowing, dharmacakra, many coming and Mahakassapa, to the rest of the poem, carried home by other hands.

how: English translations of the full Buddhacarita follow the Sanskrit where it survives and the Tibetan or Chinese versions after that; the Buddha's relics are honored at stupas across Asia.

games.q: you're one of the kings. the Buddha has died, and every kingdom wants his relics. armies are gathering. what do you do?
o: give up your claim and go home.
games.why: the kings nearly go to war, then agree to divide the relics, each carrying a portion home to honor.

practice: Let a picture come: a story copied by hand, wrapped, carried on someone's back over long roads, and read aloud somewhere new.
Then think of one story in your own life that someone else carried to you, and rest with thanks for the hands it passed through.

wordCard.voice: Final nirvana. The passing the Buddha enters in the rest of the poem, carried on in Tibetan and Chinese after the Sanskrit breaks off, after his last journey and the relics shared. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the poem traveled. Broken off in one language, it was kept in two others. Until tomorrow.
